entry.text: Two hundred metres of washing line zigzags between the dead willows, and hanging from it, pegged neatly at the shoulders, are people. Skins. Empty, cleaned, turned inside out to dry, sorted by size. There are dozens. Beneath them sits a treadle sewing machine on a dry platform, and a figure working it at speed, humming, mouth full of pins. It sees you. It takes the pins out of its mouth with great care before speaking, because it was raised properly. "Oh, thank goodness. Are you a thirty-two long?"

choices.label: Say you're just passing and admire the stitching
Cut a line down and take whatever's in the pockets

the_workshop.text: The pockets are full and the workshop is better — this thing has been collecting for a long time and it keeps a tidy shop. Bolts of waterproof canvas, a crate of tinned food, sealed thread and needles that would pass for surgical, a jerry can. Every skin on the line, you notice, is mended. Patched at the elbows. Darned at the knees. Somebody has been repairing these for years, with enormous care, and hanging them back up.

choices.label: Ask who the clothes belong to
Rob the shop while it's threading a needle

the_client.text: "Mister Adwell," the tailor says, and nods at a wicker chair you had taken for empty. It is not empty. Mister Adwell is in it: a lean, entirely alive old man in his underwear, who has been getting his skin cleaned, mended and returned to him weekly for thirty-one years, and who has opinions. "The seams pull," he says to you, conspiratorially. "I've mentioned it." The tailor says it does not pull. Mister Adwell says it pulls. This argument, you understand, is the oldest structure in the marsh. Adwell pays you in salvage to take his side. The tailor pays you in better salvage not to. You take both and leave before either notices.

fitting.text: It measures you before you can decline, and it measures fast, and two of the measurements are taken from the inside. The tailor apologises for the cold hands. It does not apologise for the rest.

line_whip.text: You cut the wrong line. Two hundred metres of tensioned wire and forty hanging people come down at once, and the wire takes you across the face on the way past. The pile lands on top of you. Some of it is still damp.

measuring_tape.text: The tailor gets excited about the question and forgets itself, and the tape goes round your throat twice while it explains. You get it off. It is mortified. You are, for about forty seconds, extremely close to being a coat.

treadle.text: Nobody works a treadle that fast by hand. Your sleeve goes under the foot and your arm follows it, and the machine puts eleven immaculate, evenly spaced stitches through your forearm before the tailor can stop pedalling. "Look at that tension, though," it says, devastated and slightly proud.
